Release
re-LEES
n. and v.t. (a remitting of debt or a setting free; rendering Hebrew shemittah, Greek apoluo)
From Old French relaissier, Latin relaxare, to loosen again. The Hebrew shemittah means a dropping or letting fall — the creditor opens his hand and the debt falls out of it.

Biblical Definition

The release is a fixed institution in Israel's law, not an occasional act of generosity: “At the end of every seven years thou shalt make a release” (Deuteronomy 15:1), and the terms are spelled out in the next verse — “Every creditor that lendeth ought unto his neighbour shall release it; he shall not exact it of his neighbour, or of his brother; because it is called the LORD'S release” (Deuteronomy 15:2). Three things are worth noting. The release is periodic and predictable, so that both borrower and lender know the calendar. It is bounded by covenant kinship — brother and neighbour, with foreigners on ordinary commercial terms. And it is titled the LORD's release, which is the whole basis of it: the money was never ultimately the creditor's, any more than the land was. Moses anticipates the obvious temptation and forbids it in the same chapter, that a man's eye be evil against his poor brother as the seventh year approaches and he refuses the loan. The word then reappears in the passion narrative with terrible irony: “at that feast the governor was wont to release unto the people a prisoner, whom they would” (Matthew 27:15). At the appointed feast, in an appointed act of release, the crowd chooses a murderer, and the innocent is bound. The pattern of substitution could not be plainer — Barabbas goes free because Jesus does not.

Webster 1828 Definition

A remitting of debt or a setting free. Deuteronomy 15 makes it a fixed sabbatical institution called the LORD's release; Matthew 27 shows Pilate's customary release used to free Barabbas and bind Christ — substitution enacted in public.

expand to see more

RELEASE, v.t. [Fr. relaisser; L. relaxo.] To set free from restraint of any kind, either physical or moral; to liberate from prison, confinement or servitude.

2. To free from pain, care, trouble, grief, &c.

3. To free from obligation or penalty; as, to release one from debt, from a promise or covenant.

4. To quit; to let go, as a legal claim; as, to release a debt or forfeiture.

RELEASE, n. Liberation from restraint; discharge from obligation, debt or penalty; as the year of release. Deut. 15.

Key Scripture

Deuteronomy 15:1 — "At the end of every seven years thou shalt make a release."

Deuteronomy 15:2 — "And this is the manner of the release: Every creditor that lendeth ought unto his neighbour shall release it; he shall not exact it of his neighbour, or of his brother; because it is called the LORD'S release."

Matthew 27:15 — "Now at that feast the governor was wont to release unto the people a prisoner, whom they would."

Deuteronomy 31:10 — "And Moses commanded them, saying, At the end of every seven years, in the solemnity of the year of release, in the feast of tabernacles,"

Modern Corruption

Deuteronomy 15 is used as a proof-text for general debt cancellation stripped of its covenantal boundaries and its accompanying command to lend generously — and in the opposite error, dismissed as expired ceremonial law with no claim on Christian mercy at all.

expand to see more

The sabbatical release is regularly enlisted for modern debt-forgiveness campaigns, and the citation usually stops before the qualifications. The law releases loans among covenant brothers, not commercial credit generally; it explicitly permits exacting from a foreigner; it presupposes an agrarian economy in which land could not be permanently alienated; and it is paired with the command not to withhold the loan in the first place as the seventh year approaches, which is a demand on the lender's heart rather than merely his ledger. Lifted out of that frame, it becomes a slogan that a creditor is a villain, which the chapter never says — the chapter says a hard-hearted creditor is a villain, and commands open-handedness before it commands cancellation.

The opposite dismissal is just as unfaithful. Israel's civil laws are not directly binding on Christians under the new covenant, and the dictionary does not pretend otherwise; but the Reformed tradition has always held that their general equity continues, which is the language the confessions use. The equity here is unmistakable: God's people are not to be creditors who grind their brothers, debt is not to become a permanent status, and the poor brother has a claim on the open hand. Paul reasons the same way in 2 Corinthians 8-9 without citing the statute. And behind both stands Matthew 27:15, where a release goes to a guilty man because an innocent one was held — the pattern of every debt actually cancelled.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew shemittah (a dropping, letting fall, hence remission), from shamat, to let drop; Greek apoluo (to loose away, dismiss, release) and aphesis (remission, forgiveness).

expand to see more

Hebrew shemittah (H8059) — a remitting, release; the technical term for the seventh-year cancellation in Deuteronomy 15:1-2, 9.

Hebrew shamat (H8058) — to let drop, release, let rest; used of the land resting in Exodus 23:11 and of Uzzah's oxen shaking the ark.

Greek apoluo (G630) — to loose from, dismiss, set free; the verb in Matthew 27:15-26, and also the word for putting away a wife.

Greek aphesis (G859) — a sending away, remission; used of forgiveness of sins and of the liberty proclaimed in Luke 4:18.

Greek apheimi (G863) — to send away, forgive, remit; the verb in the Lord's Prayer, forgive us our debts.

Usage

"“It is called the LORD'S release” — the debt is remitted on God's authority because the wealth was never absolutely the creditor's."

"“The solemnity of the year of release” — a fixed and public calendar, not private discretion."

"“The governor was wont to release… a prisoner” — Barabbas goes free because Christ is held."
